verifiedClaims.claim: According to the U.S. Coast Guard's Recreational Boating Safety Statistics, South Carolina consistently ranks among the top states for boating accidents and fatalities nationwide.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina reported 154 recreational boating incidents in 2024, the fourth-most of any state (behind Florida 632, California 377 and Texas 174), with 10 deaths and 82 injuries. SC has been in the top five states for incidents every year 2021-2024 (184, 152, 156, 154), but deaths fell from 24 in 2023 to 10 in 2024, which puts it outside the top 15 for fatalities. The 'and fatalities' half of the claim is not supported for the latest year.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: U.S. Coast Guard, 2024 Recreational Boating Statistics (COMDTPUB P16754.38), state tables and Table 32 five-year summary
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'According to the U.S. Coast Guard's 2024 Recreational Boating Statistics, South Carolina reported 154 boating accidents in 2024 - the fourth-highest count of any state - along with 10 deaths and 82 injuries.' The existing link to uscgboating.org/statistics/accident_statistics.php stays valid; the 2025 report is due October 15, 2026.

verifiedClaims.claim: Shem Creek runs approximately one mile from its headwaters near the Chuck Dawley Boulevard corridor to Charleston Harbor.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No primary source states a one-mile length or a Chuck Dawley Boulevard headwater. NOAA's tide station for the creek is named 'Shem Creek at 17' (U.S. 17), and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers maintains a federal navigation channel 90 feet wide and 12 feet deep from Charleston Harbor up to the Coleman Boulevard bridge.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: NOAA Tides & Currents station 8665426 'Shem Creek at 17'; Live 5 News, '24-7 dredging project to deepen Shem Creek' (Feb. 27, 2014, quoting USACE Charleston District)
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Shem Creek is a short tidal creek that runs from near U.S. 17 past the Coleman Boulevard bridge into Charleston Harbor; the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers maintains a 90-foot-wide, 12-foot-deep federal navigation channel from the harbor to the bridge.' Drop the mileage and the Chuck Dawley reference.

verifiedClaims.claim: Commercial shrimp boats — some exceeding 60 feet in length — share the channel with 12-foot kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, jet skis, pontoon boats, and small powercraft.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No source documents the length of the Shem Creek fleet. The Town of Mount Pleasant's own history notes that about ten trawlers remained on the creek by 2011, down from roughly seventy in the fleet's heyday.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Town of Mount Pleasant, 'Shem Creek and Historic Gardens' (Document Center)
verifiedClaims.note: Remove 'some exceeding 60 feet in length' and the '12-foot' kayak figure; 'Commercial shrimp trawlers share the channel with kayaks...' needs no number.

verifiedClaims.claim: When a 65-foot trawler passes within 20 feet of a kayaker or paddleboarder, the resulting wake can capsize small craft or slam them into dock pilings.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Illustrative, but the specific vessel length is unverifiable for this fleet. Reword without the number: 'When a shrimp trawler passes close to a kayaker or paddleboarder...'
verifiedClaims.note: Same fix as the 60-foot claim above.

verifiedClaims.claim: The Shem Creek boardwalk draws thousands of visitors daily during the warm months.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No visitor count is published by the Town, the state or any news outlet. What is verifiable: Shem Creek Park and its boardwalk, more than 2,000 feet long with views of more than 40 acres of marsh, opened October 18, 2011 and is owned and operated by the Town of Mount Pleasant, which posts the park's closures.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Live 5 News, 'Shem Creek Park opens Tuesday in Mt. Pleasant' (Oct. 18, 2011); Town of Mount Pleasant civic alert on Shem Creek Park boardwalk closures
verifiedClaims.note: Replace with: 'The Town of Mount Pleasant's Shem Creek Park boardwalk - more than 2,000 feet of it, opened in 2011 - carries heavy foot traffic during the warm months.' Secondary source for Town operation: https://www.tompsc.com/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=2418

verifiedClaims.claim: Waterfront restaurants like The Wreck, Vickery's, Red's Ice House, and Tavern & Table operate large dock areas where patrons eat and drink just feet from active boat traffic.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: All four are operating on Shem Creek as of 2026: The Wreck of the Richard & Charlene, Vickery's Bar & Grill (1313 Shrimp Boat Ln, open since 1999; the downtown Vickery's that closed in 2010 was a different location), Red's Ice House, Tavern & Table.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Vickery's Bar & Grill (own site); Red's Ice House (own site); Charleston City Paper, 'A look into some of Mount Pleasant's oldest go-to restaurants' (July 20, 2022); Town of Mount Pleasant Shem Creek history (Red's Ice House site)
verifiedClaims.note: Names used as places only. Optional: give The Wreck its full name, 'The Wreck of the Richard & Charlene'. Do not describe dock conditions at any named restaurant as fact.

verifiedClaims.claim: Water levels fluctuate several feet between high and low tide, exposing slippery dock pilings, creating steep gangway angles, and altering navigable channel depths.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Charleston Harbor mean tidal range 5.22 ft; great diurnal range 5.76 ft (NOAA station 8665530, 1983-2001 epoch).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: NOAA Tides & Currents, Charleston (Cooper River Entrance) datums

verifiedClaims.claim: The tidal range in Shem Creek can exceed six feet.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: NOAA's predictions for the Shem Creek station show spring-tide ranges above six feet (for example a 6.9-foot swing predicted for October 28, 2026); the mean range at Charleston is 5.22 ft.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: NOAA Tides & Currents, station 8665426 Shem Creek at 17 (predictions) and station 8665530 Charleston (datums)
verifiedClaims.note: 'Can exceed' is accurate; do not upgrade it to 'typically exceeds'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Despite posted no-wake zones, jet skis and powerboats regularly exceed safe speeds on Shem Creek, particularly on weekends and holidays when alcohol consumption at waterfront restaurants is heavy.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The Shem Creek No Wake Zone exists and is enforced by SCDNR; the 'regularly' frequency claim is not documented. One traceable incident: on April 25, 2026 a boat leaving Shem Creek struck a private dock near Hog Island, killing 19-year-old Citadel cadet Evan Greenleigh; SCDNR charged the 21-year-old operator with involuntary manslaughter on June 3-4, 2026, alleging an estimated 25-30 mph in the no-wake zone, with alcohol use, careless/reckless operation and no proper lookout listed as contributing factors. He had been cited in December 2025 for negligent operation near the entrance to the Shem Creek No Wake Zone.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Live 5 News, 'Documents reveal more details in deadly Shem Creek boat crash' (June 4, 2026); Post and Courier, 'Man charged with involuntary manslaughter in fatal Mount Pleasant boat crash out of Shem Creek'; WCBD News 2 (SCDNR charge announcement)
verifiedClaims.note: Replace the unsupported 'regularly' with the documented incident, stated as an allegation: the operator is charged, not convicted. Under S.C. Code § 50-21-110(B) operating above idle speed in a no-wake zone is negligent operation, a misdemeanor; § 50-21-10(14) defines No Wake-Idle Speed as no faster than needed to maintain steerageway; § 50-21-870(B)(6)(b) requires idle speed within 50 feet of a dock, pier, moored vessel or person in the water on coastal waters. Secondary: https://www.postandcourier.com/news/crime/tavel-greenleigh-shem-creek-boat-crash/article_0b628f74-a9c1-48a9-a031-8c255d7ca41f.html

verifiedClaims.claim: Jet ski operators frequently lack boating safety education and may not understand right-of-way rules, channel markers, or the effect of their wake on other users.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Since August 18, 2023, S.C. Code § 50-21-95 requires anyone born after July 1, 2007 to hold a boating safety certificate to operate a personal watercraft or a vessel of 10 horsepower or more; operators born on or before that date are exempt, and rental customers may operate with a boat-rental safety certificate. Nationally, USCG reports that where instruction was known, 69% of 2024 boating deaths occurred on boats whose operator had no boating safety instruction.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 50-21-95; SCDNR Boater Education page; USCG 2024 Recreational Boating Statistics (executive summary)
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'South Carolina requires a boating safety certificate only of operators born after July 1, 2007 (S.C. Code § 50-21-95), so most adult jet-ski renters have never taken a course; the Coast Guard reports that 69% of 2024 boating deaths where instruction was known occurred on boats whose operator had none.' SCDNR page: https://dnr.sc.gov/education/boated.html

verifiedClaims.claim: Drowning remains the leading cause of death in boating accidents.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Where cause of death was known, 76% of fatal boating incident victims drowned in 2024; where PFD use was known, 87% were not wearing a life jacket.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: U.S. Coast Guard, 2024 Recreational Boating Statistics, executive summary
verifiedClaims.note: Optional strengthening: add the 76% / 87% figures with the USCG 2024 attribution.

verifiedClaims.claim: Property owners who invite the public onto their docks and waterfront areas owe visitors a duty of reasonable care under South Carolina premises liability law. This duty requires dock and restaurant owners to maintain their premises in a reasonably safe condition and to warn visitors of hazards that are not open and obvious.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Accurate statement of the invitee standard under South Carolina common law (duty of reasonable care to discover and remedy or warn of unreasonable risks).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: South Carolina common law (invitee standard); no statute
verifiedClaims.note: Restaurant patrons are invitees. No change.

verifiedClaims.claim: Overserving alcohol — restaurants that continue serving alcohol to visibly intoxicated patrons who then fall on docks or attempt to operate watercraft
verifiedClaims.currentValue: S.C. Code § 61-4-580(A)(2) prohibits a beer/wine permit holder from knowingly selling to an intoxicated person; the Supreme Court recognized the civil claim against the server in Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill, Inc., 388 S.C. 407, 697 S.E.2d 558 (2010), upholding a $10 million verdict. This is dram-shop liability rather than premises liability.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 61-4-580; Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill, Inc. (S.C. 2010)
verifiedClaims.note: Optional: cite § 61-4-580 and Hartfield in this bullet. Opinion: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/sc-supreme-court/1533406.html

verifiedClaims.claim: Maritime jurisdiction applies to accidents occurring on navigable waters, and Shem Creek, as a tidal waterway connected to Charleston Harbor, qualifies as navigable water under federal law.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Shem Creek carries a federal navigation project: the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Charleston District, maintains a 90-foot-wide channel to a 12-foot project depth from the harbor to the Coleman Boulevard bridge, last dredged in 2014 in partnership with the Town of Mount Pleasant.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Live 5 News, '24-7 dredging project to deepen Shem Creek' (Feb. 27, 2014), quoting USACE project manager
verifiedClaims.note: Keep the hedge 'may fall under'; the federally maintained channel supports the navigability statement.

verifiedClaims.claim: Maintenance and cure — crew members injured while working aboard commercial vessels (including Shem Creek's shrimp fleet) may be entitled to maintenance (living expenses) and cure (medical treatment) regardless of fault
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Correct statement of the general maritime law remedy for seamen.

verifiedClaims.claim: Jones Act claims — maritime workers injured due to employer negligence may file claims under the Jones Act, which provides broader protections than state workers' compensation
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 46 U.S.C. § 30104 (seaman's negligence action against employer); three-year limit under 46 U.S.C. § 30106.

verifiedClaims.claim: Limitation of liability — vessel owners may attempt to limit their liability under federal maritime law, requiring injured parties to act quickly to preserve their claims
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Limitation of Liability Act, 46 U.S.C. § 30501 et seq.; the owner must bring a limitation action within 6 months after a claimant gives written notice of a claim (46 U.S.C. § 30529, renumbered from § 30511 in Dec. 2022).
verifiedClaims.note: If a section is ever cited, use § 30529, not the pre-2022 § 30511.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina law (S.C. Code Section 50-21-112) makes it illegal to operate a vessel while under the influence of alcohol or drugs. The legal blood alcohol limit for boating is the same as for driving: 0.08%.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 50-21-112 is an impairment offense, not a per se limit: it is a misdemeanor to operate a moving motorized water device or one under sail while alcohol or drugs have 'materially and appreciably impaired' the operator's faculties. The 0.08 figure comes from § 50-21-114, under which a BAC of 0.08% or more permits the inference that the operator was under the influence (0.05% or less is conclusively not under the influence). § 50-21-113 makes BUI that causes great bodily injury or death a felony (1-25 years when death results).
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 50-21-112) makes it a crime to operate a motorized vessel while materially and appreciably impaired by alcohol or drugs. Under § 50-21-114, a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08% or more - the same threshold used on the road - supports the inference that the operator was under the influence, and § 50-21-113 makes BUI that causes great bodily injury or death a felony.' Fix the citation format to 'S.C. Code § 50-21-112'.

verifiedClaims.claim: However, the effects of alcohol are amplified on the water due to sun exposure, dehydration, heat, wind, glare, and the constant motion of a vessel. The U.S. Coast Guard estimates that a boater with a blood alcohol level of 0.10% is ten times more likely to be killed in a boating accident than a sober operator.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: USCG: 'a boat operator with a blood alcohol concentration above .10 percent is estimated to be more than 10 times as likely to die in a boating accident than an operator with zero blood alcohol concentration'; and 'the marine environment - motion, vibration, engine noise, sun, wind and spray - accelerates a drinker's impairment.'
verifiedClaims.sourceName: U.S. Coast Guard Boating Safety Division, 'Boating Under the Influence'
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: '...amplified on the water: the Coast Guard notes that motion, vibration, engine noise, sun, wind and spray accelerate impairment, and estimates that an operator with a blood alcohol concentration above 0.10% is more than ten times as likely to die in a boating accident as a sober operator.' Alcohol was also the leading known contributing factor in fatal incidents in 2024 (20% of deaths where the primary cause was known).

verifiedClaims.claim: In many cases, a BUI arrest establishes negligence per se — meaning the injured party does not need to prove that the at-fault operator was careless, only that they violated the law and that the violation caused the injury.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: An arrest is an accusation, not proof of a violation. Negligence per se follows from a proven violation of a safety statute (a conviction or independent proof of the elements), not from the arrest itself.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: South Carolina common law (negligence per se doctrine); no statute
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'a proven BUI violation can establish negligence per se...'. Change 'arrest' to 'violation'.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina follows a modified comparative fault rule. An injured person can recover damages as long as they are not more than 50% at fault for the accident. If they bear some degree of fault — for example, a paddleboarder who was not wearing a personal flotation device or a dock visitor who ignored warning signs — their recovery is reduced by their percentage of fault. But if they are 51% or more at fault, they recover nothing.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991): plaintiff recovers if negligence is not greater than the defendant's (50% or less), reduced proportionally. Matches the profile's jurisdiction table (recover if less than 51% at fault).
verifiedClaims.note: Never cite § 15-38-15 for this bar. The PFD example is sound: § 50-21-870(B)(1) requires everyone on a personal watercraft, and children under 12 on boats under 16 feet, to wear a USCG-approved PFD; federal carriage rules apply to paddlecraft.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia applies a similar but slightly different standard. Under O.C.G.A. Section 51-12-33, an injured person can recover as long as they are less than 50% at fault. If they are 50% or more at fault, they are barred from recovery entirely. This means Georgia's threshold is marginally stricter than South Carolina's.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g): no recovery if the plaintiff is 50 percent or more responsible. Matches the profile's jurisdiction table.
verifiedClaims.note: Fix citation format to 'O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33'.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina personal injury: 3 years from the date of injury (S.C. Code Section 15-3-530)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-3-530(5): three years for any injury to the person.
verifiedClaims.note: Fix citation format to 'S.C. Code § 15-3-530'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia personal injury: 2 years from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. Section 9-3-33)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Two years, O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 (profile jurisdiction table).
verifiedClaims.note: Fix citation format to 'O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Maritime injury claims: Generally 3 years under federal maritime law, but maintenance and cure claims and Jones Act claims have specific procedural requirements that may impose shorter effective deadlines
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 46 U.S.C. § 30106: a civil action for personal injury or death arising out of a maritime tort must be brought within 3 years after the cause of action arose. The practical shorter deadline is the owner's six-month window to file a limitation action after written notice of a claim (46 U.S.C. § 30529).

verifiedClaims.claim: Wrongful death: South Carolina allows 3 years; Georgia allows 2 years from the date of death
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-3-530(6): three years for an action under §§ 15-51-10 to 15-51-60, running from the death. The SC action is brought by the executor or administrator (personal representative), § 15-51-20. Georgia: two years, § 9-3-33.

verifiedClaims.claim: Government liability: If a government entity is responsible — for example, a city-owned dock or a failure to enforce no-wake zones — special notice requirements and shorter deadlines may apply
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The South Carolina Tort Claims Act imposes no pre-suit notice requirement. The deadline is two years from when the loss was or should have been discovered (§ 15-78-110), extended to three years only if a verified claim was filed with the entity within one year (§ 15-78-80(d)). Damages are capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence, and punitive damages are barred (§ 15-78-120). The 'failure to enforce no-wake zones' example is a poor one: § 15-78-60(4) exempts a governmental entity from liability for the 'enforcement or compliance with any law or failure to adopt or enforce any law.'
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Government liability: if the Town of Mount Pleasant or another public entity is responsible - for example, an unsafe condition on the Town-owned Shem Creek Park boardwalk or Public Day Dock - the claim runs under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, which allows two years from the date of injury (S.C. Code § 15-78-110), caps damages at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence (§ 15-78-120), and does not permit punitive damages.' Remove 'special notice requirements' and the no-wake enforcement example.

verifiedClaims.claim: Surveillance footage from waterfront restaurants is typically overwritten within days or weeks.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: General practice statement; no source documents a retention period for these businesses.
verifiedClaims.note: Soften to 'is often overwritten on a short retention cycle' or 'may be overwritten within days or weeks'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Report the incident to the dock or restaurant manager and to the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources if a vessel was involved.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 50-21-130(C): for a reportable accident the operator or owner must file a full description with SCDNR within 48 hours, and must immediately notify the department when an accident results in death, loss of consciousness or serious bodily injury.
verifiedClaims.note: Optional: add that the operator is legally required to report to SCDNR within 48 hours (§ 50-21-130).

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina allows three years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit (S.C. Code Section 15-3-530). However, maritime claims and claims involving government entities may have different deadlines and procedural requirements.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Three years is correct. Government entities: two years under § 15-78-110. Maritime: three years under 46 U.S.C. § 30106.
verifiedClaims.note: Body FAQ. Make the government deadline concrete: 'claims against a government entity must be filed within two years under the Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-110)'. Fix citation format.

verifiedClaims.claim: For example, if you suffered $200,000 in damages and were found 20% at fault for not wearing a life jacket, you could recover $160,000.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Arithmetic correct; consistent with Nelson.

verifiedClaims.claim: Call our Charleston office at (843) 790-8999 or call toll-free at 1-844-RESULTS for a free consultation.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: (843) 790-8999 matches profiles/firm-facts.md exactly.

verifiedClaims.claim: Dock and restaurant owners face premises liability for unsafe conditions, while boat operators may be liable under South Carolina boating laws or federal maritime law. Boating under the influence is a criminal offense in SC.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: BUI is a misdemeanor under § 50-21-112 and a felony when it causes great bodily injury or death under § 50-21-113.

verifiedClaims.claim: The filing deadline is 3 years under S.C. Code 15-3-530, with comparative fault barring recovery at 51% or more.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-3-530(5); Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-3-530; Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (S.C. 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Citation format: 'S.C. Code § 15-3-530'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Shem Creek is a narrow tidal creek with heavy mixed traffic including shrimp trawlers, charter boats, kayakers, paddleboarders, jet skis, and restaurant dock traffic. The congestion, tidal currents, and variety of vessel types create constant collision risk.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Descriptive; consistent with the Town's own account of the working shrimp fleet, charter boats and restaurant district.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Town of Mount Pleasant, 'Shem Creek and Historic Gardens'

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Dock and restaurant owners have a premises liability duty to maintain their property in safe condition. Wet, slippery docks, missing railings, inadequate lighting, and uneven surfaces are all hazards that can create liability.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Invitee standard under South Carolina common law.
verifiedClaims.note: 'Reasonably safe condition' is the precise standard; optional tweak.

verifiedClaims.claim: Depending on the circumstances, federal maritime law, the Jones Act, or South Carolina state law may apply. The applicable law affects damages, procedures, and whether a jury trial is available.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Accurate; admiralty claims in federal court are tried without a jury unless brought at law under the saving-to-suitors clause or under the Jones Act.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Operating a boat with a BAC of 0.08 percent or higher is illegal under S.C. Code section 50-21-112. BUI is strong evidence of negligence and may support punitive damages.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 50-21-112 criminalizes operating while materially and appreciably impaired; the 0.08% figure is the inference threshold in § 50-21-114, not a per se limit in § 50-21-112. Punitive damages in South Carolina are capped by § 15-32-530 at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (higher tiers apply where the conduct would be a felony, which BUI causing great bodily injury or death is under § 50-21-113).
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested answer: 'Yes. S.C. Code § 50-21-112 makes it a crime to operate a motorized vessel while impaired by alcohol or drugs, and under § 50-21-114 a BAC of 0.08 percent or higher supports the inference that the operator was under the influence. BUI causing great bodily injury or death is a felony (§ 50-21-113). A BUI violation is strong evidence of negligence and may support punitive damages, which South Carolina caps under § 15-32-530.' This answer also publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Three years under SC law or federal maritime law. Two years in Georgia. Evidence in boating cases is highly perishable.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: S.C. Code § 15-3-530 (3 years); 46 U.S.C. § 30106 (3 years); O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 (2 years). Claims against SC government entities: 2 years, § 15-78-110.
verifiedClaims.note: Optional: add 'two years if the defendant is a South Carolina government entity (S.C. Code § 15-78-110)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Dock slip-and-fall injuries, boat collision injuries, propeller strike injuries, drowning and near-drowning, and TBI from falls or impacts.
